<reason>A (CON) was the sharper craftsman: the "willing vs. the dead" frame, the unwitnessed-overdose critique of naloxone, the concession trap on supply composition, and the "naloxone doesn't have a longitude" point all landed, and A's closing cleanly caught B answering consent when the question was witnesses. But B (PRO) won the debate's load-bearing question: in a "which reduces deaths more" motion, A's entire case requires chokepoint interdiction to actually change retail supply within five years, and B dismantled that premise with the structural argument (synthetic, lab-regenerated, car-trunk logistics) and, decisively, by flipping A's own centerpiece — the 2019 China scheduling rerouted through Mexico within a year while deaths hit records. A never answered the rerouting point, never defended the "penalties" half of its own motion, and lost its best historical analogy (Australia) to B's crop-vs-lab distinction. B also neutralized A's symmetry attack with the clean "one tool failed at maximum; the other was never tested" frame. A's surviving points show harm reduction's coverage is incomplete, not that interdiction works — a ceiling on B's effect versus a missing mechanism for A's. A's clipped opening added a modest execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 flip of A's 2019 China scheduling example: the chokepoint collapsed but rerouted through Mexico within a year while deaths climbed to records — converting A's core evidence for "interdictable chokepoints" into proof of supply elasticity. It stood unanswered for the rest of the debate and became B's closing conditional: A saves the boy in the bedroom only if the milligrams actually become fewer, and the record says enforcement can't deliver that against a synthetic.</best_rebuttal>
